full_text:
Interviewer:	I'll start off telling you a bit about what we're doing then it'll make sense to you. We're interviewing women from all the different engineering disciplines, mainly people who are going on placement – did you say that you're going on placement?

Subject:	Yeah

Interviewer:	We're trying to find out a bit about why they decided to do engineering and their experiences of the course so far, and what they hope to get out of their placement as well. There's a lot of research recently that says that more women are doing engineering but they tend to drop out after a while. So we're trying to look at ways of improving retention of women in the industry. So, at the end of the 2 year project, we're going to put together a document to give to the engineering councils and hopefully improve the situation for women in the industry. I'll start off asking you a few background questions about why you decided to do engineering. Is it mechanical engineering that you're doing?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	What 'A' levels did you do?

Subject:	Maths – maths at 'AS', physics and English Lit.

Interviewer:	OK, and what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Bog standard

Interviewer:	It wasn't an all girls school?

Subject:	No – comprehensive school

Interviewer:	Ok, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

Subject:	Well, I did like a two weeks placement, you know – like your normal work experience that you do at sixth form I did in an engineering place.

Interviewer:	OK. What do your parents do? Are either of them engineers at all?

Subject:	Erm, my dad's not technically an engineer, he's a design draughtsman, but it's kind of – he works for an engineering firm.

Interviewer:	Yeah, sort of in the industry. OK when and why do you think that you decided to do engineering at university?

Subject:	Er, well after my placement – I decided to do my placement – because the first placement I did was accounting and it was so boring – completely be boring and I was like I want to do something mathematical but more applied, so if you go down the physics line as well, its going to be the obvious choice isn't it. And because, once you've got an engineering degree, you don't have to be an engineer (OK) so I'm keeping it open.

Interviewer:	Oh good, do you think anything else influenced your decision to study engineering, like your interests or the fact that your dad was in industry or any careers advice that you've had?

Subject:	My dad tried to put me off it, if anything, because he really hates his job. Erm, careers advice was – well, non-existent really. There was nothing to it. I suppose it was my own decision but I really don't know on what influenced it.

Interviewer:	Your dad didn't put you off though?

Subject:	No. Well after I'd done my placement I was like yeah, this is so much more interesting than the stuff you're doing.

Interviewer:	OK, when you decided you did want to do engineering, did you do much research into it, or did you speak to any other engineers or anything like that?

Subject:	Erm, I kind of got in touch with a guy, who got me my placement and basically what he said was, you know, get an engineering degree then you've got so many options that you're not tying yourself down – so go for it.

Interviewer:	OK, What do you think it is that appeals to you about engineering?

Subject:	Erm, probably the hands-on ishness. It's not just sat in a lab, you do get to do other things as well.

Interviewer:	OK, why do you think you decided to do mechanical engineering and not civil engineering or something in one of the other disciplines? Did you ever consider doing any of the others?

Subject:	I considered electrical, cos I kind of want to do mechatronic, but I couldn't find a uni that did a good mechatronic course, whereas mechanical you get mechatronic elements in it anyway. So it's like if you select those modules, you can get mechatronics basically.

Interviewer:	And what is it – that specifically? You know, about – mechatronics?

Subject:	Er, toys.- play (?) – I suppose it's like – it's new technology, isn't it really – things like something to play with, I'm such a little kid.

Interviewer:	When you applied to the course, did you know you wanted to do a placement year?

Subject:	No. [This university] was my last choice.

Interviewer:	Was it?

Subject:	 (?) and it was well, it was, [university 2] was my first choice and they wouldn't take me. And [this university] had already confirmed that they'd take me basically, whatever I got, so I rang them up and they were like yeah, so I thought I'll just go to [this university].

Interviewer:	Were you upset that you didn't get to go to [university 2] though?

Subject:	Er, not really. Erm, I wasn't actually that bothered between all six anyway anyway. But [university 2] had a better reputation than [this university] because it had the lowest grades but I figured wherever I went it'd be good fun.

Interviewer:	Did you realise that engineering was so male dominated when you decided to do it?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Does it ever bother you at all?

Subject:	Nah, at school like my maths class I was the only girl. In physics there was two of us, you get used to it. I did electronics at GCSE, I was the only girl on that – it really didn't make a difference.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

Subject:	Not purely because they're female. If they're gonna be good engineers they'll go for it but …

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women don't do engineering, not because they don't even know what it is, to be interested in it in the first place?

Subject:	Yeah, I guess quite a lot of places – a lot of people wouldn't think of it or suggesting it to the girls. Whereas, my school – they kind of give you the chances and they knew what I was like anyway. But yeah, it could be like more education or…

Interviewer:	OK, What characteristics then, do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Erm, probably slightly strange (laugher). You've got to like playing with things and playing about with things and practical. Anyone who sits down and takes something apart – basically will make a good engineer, cos they'll know how things will work. I suppose that's (?) – you have to know what makes things work.

Interviewer:	Do you think that men are generally more like that than women?

Subject:	Erm, well some are but then some women are like it as well. I guess it's the way you've been brought up rather than the natural male/female thing.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there is a perception though?

Subject:	Yeah, I guess so. If you break something you take it to daddy, not mummy don't you.

Interviewer:	OK, Do you think that there are any advantages or disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Loads of advantages. 

Interviewer:	What?

Subject:	If you're sat in a lab, and you can't do it, and you go, I'm really stuck, and I don't really understand – they'll help you. All the lads are just like, he didn't tell me that. You're like well, tough. Yeah, you can get away with a lot more, and I think there is a perception that you've done more as well, so they'll give you more help, they will. And girls don't mind asking, in like the group of us there's like me and [name] and then there's like 6 lads and they'll be like oh I'll work it out now, and if you just ask they'll tell you and – but none of the lads'll ask, so you do get away with more but then you add something as well so…

Interviewer:	Ok, what about any disadvantages?

Subject:	Sorry?

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any disadvantages?

Subject:	Erm, well I guess it's the same that you're perceived to be dumber, so depending on what company you're applying to, and what lecturers you've got and stuff. I know there's one lecturer who does sort of go, ooh, you're a girl, and again I suppose if you're applying for jobs you might be disadvantaged but then again, a lot of people are looking for female engineers now, aren't they? So it's usually an advantage.

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of the course then, has it been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Pretty much – yeah. I mean I went through a lot of it on open day and stuff anyway but…

Interviewer:	How many women are on your course?

Subject:	Erm, 15 maybe – I don't really know.

Interviewer:	Out of how many?

Subject:	I think 20. It seems really high.

Interviewer:	That's fine. What would you say have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Best things are design modules because you get to play. The worst things is Maths, because it's just pure calculations and no application whatsoever.

Interviewer:	Is it hard then to see how it fits in with everything?

Subject:	Yeah. Well some of it, you can see how it fits in. Some of it you're like we did this at 'A' level and it didn't apply to anything then and we're doing it again and it still doesn't apply to anything now.

Interviewer:	On the whole though, are you pleased then that you did choose this course?

Subject:	Yeah. It's going to be a degree worth having, rather than I don't know, walking out with something that you haven't put any effort into and you're just…

Interviewer:	OK. Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	How many?

Subject:	One, I think. The – might be one in the first year. I think there is only one so…

Interviewer:	Do you think that the female lecturers have a different style of teaching or have you noticed that they teach a different type of subject or do you not sort of like …?

Subject:	I don't mean to generalise with you know, her –but she was very hormonal, she was pregnant. So, yeah, she taught for (thermo?) and we have like 6 (thermo?) lecturers and she was one of them. But she didn't teach the easy bits, by any means.

Interviewer:	Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	Er, not a lot – I'm not really bothered. The percentage of girls on the course, you expect it to be the same for lecturers really.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the lecturers treat the students equally? You've said a bit already about some of them.

Subject:	Yeah. Most of them will, up to a point. I mean if you blatantly push the fact that you're a girl – they will treat you differently.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do many people on your course do that?

Subject:	There is some really girly girls. My house mate was a really girly girl, but she dropped out. But she was like all pink, blonde, get away with anything kind of girl. But yeah, no not really. I mean some of them do but you don't know if it's just cos you're you, or cos you're female. 'Cos they treat everyone differently anyway, I don't really think it's a male/female thing, it's more of a what you push sort of thing.

Interviewer:	OK. Have you got a personal tutor then?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	He's male.

Interviewer:	Do you get on with them, are they approachable?

Subject:	Yeah, he's lovely.

Interviewer:	Yeah, you wouldn't rather have a female tutor?

Subject:	I'm not bothered at all.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course? 

Subject:	Erm, probably my tutor because he understands what it – you know, I failed a module in my first year and I rang him in the middle of the summer holidays, and he was like, you knew you'd fail one of them anyway, and he was really cool and…

Interviewer:	So he encouraged you?

Subject:	Yeah, he was really practical as well, he was like you know, you failed it but you know you've got a back up, you know you can do it, now you've got one exam to revise for all summer, get on and do it, type of thing.

Interviewer:	OK have you had to do much group work as part of your course?

Subject:	Er, yes, I've had a few projects.

Interviewer:	Do you like doing group work?

Subject:	Depends who you do it with. The groups you pick are fine because you get (reasonable?) people – if it's one you've been put into, it's like really frustrating if you're put with people that really don't care.

Interviewer:	How often do you get put into groups and how often do you get to choose?

Subject:	Erm, I think you get about 3 projects a year and this year we've been – well one of them we completely chose, one of them you sort of – you can choose out of so many people, one of them they picked completely for you.

Interviewer:	OK, so it's mixed.

Subject:	Yeah, it's pretty even.

Interviewer:	OK, when you get to choose who you want to work with then, how do you decide who to work with?

Subject:	I basically work with people you sit with in lectures – so I've got – well I did have 3 housemates – and people who lived next door – 3 house mates and then there's 4 other people as well and we usually just pick randomly between ourselves, for (?) or whatever.

Interviewer:	OK, and do you have a preference whether you work with men or women?

Subject:	Nah, I usually work with [male student] 'cos he's clever.

Interviewer:	Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

Subject:	Erm, again I think it just depends on the personality of the people. I mean they obviously do, but I think it's me as me rather than me as a female that makes the difference.

Interviewer:	OK, have you had any particularly bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Not yet. We've had better groups than others but we've been lucky in that every group's just had like 1 person that doesn't care, so everyone else just covers for them, whatever and it doesn't make a lot of difference. I'm sure if you're put in a group and there's like 3 people that didn't care and me, I'd be right!

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think are like the benefits of doing group work?

Subject:	I think if you get stuck you've got someone else to do it for you, basically. But it's not all your responsibility. If you work together you can get anything done, can't you?

Interviewer:	Do you think it will benefit you when you go to work in the industry, as well?

Subject:	It should do. I don't know.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anything about the teaching or advice that you've had that will help you when you go on placement?

Subject:	Erm, well a lot of – just like – I suppose it's projects that help it because you're going to be on projects, on placement, so I guess it's them that's gonna effect you know, how you go about problems and stuff like that.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you will use a lot of the technical stuff as well?

Subject:	Erm, well from what I've heard from other people, it's – none of the technical stuff applies. They completely – they teach you what they want you to know, they don't really bother with the theory at all, it's your other skills that they go on.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the course should be geared more for preparing you for going into the industry?

Subject:	I think it'd be impossible, really purely because of the number of different placements there is – if you geared it towards say automotive placements and everyone else would be completely screwed anyway, so if you do it generally you know. I mean you obviously are gonna use some of the stuff we've learnt, it's just not all of it.

Interviewer:	OK, Do you feel like you're ready and prepared to go on placement really?

Subject:	Yeah, I'm fine. To get out and do something, for a change.

Interviewer:	Do you think that, the way that you're taught, and the whole educational experience will reflect what it's like, at all, in industry?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	What do you think will be different?

Subject:	9 till 5, Monday to Friday. Even the whole, having to be there and – 'cos with lectures you can kind of get there and sleep through a few and not really pay attention. You know what you're getting – this is a business lecture and it's going to be boring, whereas in industry it's going to be non-stop. I mean you're like gonna get slack periods and stuff, but you're gonna have to work, from the time you're there, is the impression I get. But then, I'm basing this on most people – I know quite a lot of older people, like people who graduated last year and stuff that did placements – I'm basing this on quite a lot of theirs.

Interviewer:	Have you found it helpful talking to people that have the experience of working?

Subject:	Yeah – yeah, definitely.

Interviewer:	Are they people that are your friends sort of anyway?

Subject:	Yeah, well my boyfriend's an engineer, but he's a chemical engineer and there's quite a lot of people in Canoe club who were on placements last year, or the year before or whatever, so.

Interviewer:	OK, Why do you think you wanted to go on placement?

Subject:	So much fun - Just to get out and do something practical and learn something real rather than sit down and do – I mean the theory is like – it's got to be useful otherwise we wouldn't be learning it, I guess but it does seem a bit irrelevant and our projects, like well, yes, I 'm setting you this project, but we know what the answer is because we did it last year and the year before that and the year before that, whereas in industry, you know, it's something new that you're doing and it's actually got some value to someone.

Interviewer:	Do you think it'll help you put into context all the stuff you've learnt, as well?

Subject:	I'm sure it should do. We'll see.

Interviewer:	OK, has anyone particularly encouraged or discouraged you from going on placement?

Subject:	Erm, my tutor told me it'd be good. My dad told me – I think my dad told me it'd be good. Erm, but yeah it was basically people who'd been on it before – they were like you know, it's such a good experience you know. You don't come back with any money but you know so much more, you know, and you're ready to get a job.

Interviewer:	Do you know anyone that's chosen not to go on placement?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that they decided not to do a placement?

Subject:	Well he chose not to because he paddles for England and basically he spends so much time, out in – I think he took a couple of years out before he started uni and stuff like that to compete – so it's time.

Interviewer:	OK, do you don't know where you're going on your placement yet?

Subject:	I do know, I'm going to [company] (lost words)

Interviewer:	OK, and what attracted you to them?

Subject:	Er, well originally and honestly I applied to anyone that looked like it could be fun. I didn't bother on the whole, I thought yeah that'd be a good place and then I went that'll be – you know – it would look good on my CV that, I want to have had an interesting year. And they have so much variety and you know they send you round the different departments – all engineering, so you weren't like spending hours in management or anything, so you got to see different parts of what they did, so – so I wasn't really sure what I want to do when I graduate, so I thought if I go there, get a good experience and then it might – at least it narrows it down like I don't want to do that or I do want to do that.

Interviewer:	Yeah, so you think it will help you decide what you want to do when you finish? Er, so there'll be quite a lot of variety in what you're doing as well. OK, where did you find out about the companies that you applied to?

Subject:	It was all through erm [placement co-ordinator].

Interviewer:	OK are you happy with all the help that the university's given you finding a placement?

Subject:	Yeah, I think they give you loads of help. Apart from the fact that I wasn't on the list to start off with so I got all the emails.

Interviewer:	Do you think that they should be doing anything else to help?

Subject:	No, I think – if you go to the office and ask they're really helpful and basically they shouldn't be handing it to you on a plate. If you want to know stuff, you should have to get off your bum and go ask – they send you the original emails, so if you're interested and you want to know more, you should have to actively go and find out about it.

Interviewer:	It does sound like your department actually gives quite a lot of help, compared to some of the other departments?

Subject:	Well Chem eng. They match you up with them, and say like you go to one interview and you've got it made. At least we have to apply.

Interviewer:	People in design technology are only just compiling their CV's and stuff.

Subject:	Really? Yeah, well we do a lot of – I suppose it's 'cos they've got such good links anyway, in industry, that they get so many people actively coming to the uni, and saying, have you got any engineers that we can have, so.

Interviewer:	That's really good. What sorts of things are you hoping to get out of your placement then?

Subject:	Erm, the whole working experience, basically. I really don't know what to expect, because I was like do you know what I'll be doing like – they were like we don't know what projects will be in when you start, so you have to wait and see, but the actual experience of work and real life.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you'll have the opportunity to use what you've learnt, when you come back for your final year?

Subject:	Er, I hope so. I don't know whether I actually will because it depends on how many projects I do as well.

Interviewer:	Might what you do on placement help you make your mind up what you're going to do for your end of year project

Subject:	I expect it will decide me one way or the other. If I really hate it I'll know I won't do that.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think will be the worst and best things or what are you most looking forward to and most worried about on placement?

Subject:	Erm, I'm looking forward to just getting in there and actually doing something, and having responsibility and stuff. I'm not really worried about anything, at the moment. I'm sure when I get closer I will be, but at the moment, it's a couple of months away and it's sort of like (??)

Interviewer:	OK, and do the company take other students or will you be the only one?

Subject:	Yeah there's – well there's 2 departments and there's 2 guys over the road, I think, and 2 guys with me.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that will be useful having other students there?

Subject:	Yeah, well it gives you like people to rent a house with and stuff – there's that. They're obviously used to taking on students so they know how to treat them and stuff, which is – you know, basically, you're not the first one.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Have you found somewhere to live yet?

Subject:	No. But the give you like the first 4 weeks to sort it out, so basically you go into bed and breakfast - they pay for it and everything, you're just like we'll get together then and look.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that you'll get treated differently, being at work to being at university?

Subject:	What you mean – yeah – you're gonna – hopefully, they're gonna treat you like a proper employee and give you responsibility and you know expect you to do it, whereas here you get the impression that's it's just like well, oh they're students, you know, they're lazy and they're not gonna bother sort of thing.

Interviewer:	When you're working do you think that they will treat you like another student or ..?

Subject:	Well judging by people who are there – there was two people on placement there, that we talked to when we went for interview and they were like yeah, you know, give you stuff, sit down and get on with it, and if you can't – you know, they help you through it but they expect you to pave your own way, sort of thing.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK, in terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

Subject:	Up North. Not working down south. Erm, yeah, hopefully I'll be chartered and earning money.

Interviewer:	Yeah, what about say in 10 years time?

Subject:	Doing the same things, hopefully earning slightly more money but yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, would you like to go into management?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Stay on the more technical side?

Subject:	Yeah, one because I'm a technical expert – I don't ever want to do management.

Interviewer:	OK, what then would be your ideal career?

Subject:	Playing with robots. I really want to play with robots, just like all day every day.

Interviewer:	Is that a realistic option in what you want to do?

Subject:	Yeah. Yeah, well if you went across to the mechatronics rather than the mechanical (yeah) it's very feasible that you could do something like robotic arms or something anyway – maybe not normal robots but yeah, robotic arms going to need (??)

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that now you'll encounter any difficulties at all, trying to achieve that?

Subject:	I'm sure I will. But I dunno what they'll be but it's not going to be pie on a plate.

Interviewer:	OK, would you like to work abroad at all?

Subject:	Erm, if they speak English, I'll be fine. I'm not really that bothered. I go travelling when I go paddling abroad and stuff, erm and if they want to send me abroad that's fine but …

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in engineering at the minute?

Subject:	I hope so. Erm, yeah I guess so. You're always going to need engineers aren't you?

Interviewer:	What about once you're in the industry for like moving up the career ladder? Do you think the opportunities are good there?

Subject:	I guess it's the same as everyone else's at the time I want to move.

Interviewer:	OK, that's fine - are you happy with all the career choices that you've made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

Subject:	I'd do slightly more work at 'A' levels. Not to go to a different uni, but just so I knew the stuff now, because now it's just like, well, I know I did that but I can't actually remember, and having to go back and re-learn that before you do the other stuff. Yeah, I'd do more work – apart from that….

Interviewer:	OK. What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the engineering industry?

Subject:	Erm, technical, erm hard working – that's 2 – slightly crazy.

Interviewer:	Why?

Subject:	You'll always get – 'cos you get very involved people. You know you get the slightly eccentric lecturers, like we had one today that had got a rice pudding tin, drilled a hole in it, got the rice pudding out, filled it with like some sort of fuel and he set a match to it, in the middle of the lecture and we were like – great one – and it's like oh, I should have safety goggles on for this but never mind. You always get the slightly eccentric people and I think you seem to get more eccentric engineers than most other things. 

Interviewer:	Would you describe it as masculine?

Subject:	I suppose I should – I suppose I should, yeah, but I don't see it like that but I don't know if that's 'cos I'm trying to sort of integrate into it, but I'm trying to block myself seeing it like that sort of thing – you know deny the fact that its masculine – but I suppose it is, just the sheer numbers.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it is just the sheer numbers of males in the industry that make it masculine?

Subject:	Oh yeah.

Interviewer:	Or is it the type of work that's being done and the whole sort of ingrained culture?

Subject:	Well it is kind of the ingrained culture but it is over 50 years. If you had half and half male/female you wouldn't still say oh it's masculine, because the females have taken over. It is yeah – it really is the culture but it's because it's male that the culture's like that.

Interviewer:	Yeah, you said earlier that one of your house mates dropped out and that she was a girly girl, do you think that there's like this perception that if you are a woman and that you're an engineer, women can look after the height of femininity a bit to get on.

Subject:	And we see – she was well lazy anyway, so she was never gonna make it, but then [Sophie] (pseudonym), you've met, she's like a girly girl as well – she does the whole (?) and stuff, she's a really good engineer.

Interviewer:	OK, that's fine. Do you think the fact that it's masculine, will cause any problems at all?

Subject:	I don't think it will now. I think it might have done 10 years ago, but now people are leaning towards female engineers. So, there's more men about you know, actively trying to employ them, to get the numbers of accepting them in more, and everywhere you go there's probably already been a female engineer that – before you – who's like paved the way. But yes, you don't have so much work to do.

Interviewer:	Do you think that maybe women sometimes do have to work harder, to prove that they can do it?

Subject:	In certain situations yeah. Especially if you are the first or one of the first. I know when I went on my work experience placement and I first went down to shop floor. There was quite a lot of engineering (?) but when you went down to the fitters there weren't any. Well, at the first day that was when I was proving, yeah, I could do exactly what they could do and you know, I could wander round in my boiler suit and my hard hat and have a go just like them.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think the situation will improve for women?

Subject:	Yeah, just cos of the sheer number, yeah. Every year there's more women going into it, and in theory, in the end you should get half and half, shouldn't you?

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think that your educational experiences differ from other students, say in humanities or social sciences?

Subject:	Yes, I do more work.

Interviewer:	Do you think that's the main difference or…?

Subject:	What do you mean?

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the fact that you have to do more lectures and things like that, do you think that will help prepare you more for going into the industry, the fact that you have a more structured timetable?

Subject:	Erm, in certain ways, yeah but in other ways they've got to do more reading on their own because I suppose it's gonna be easier to work on your own. I think the way the course is structured helps you what – going into the industry that it's made for, so I suppose that's the difference.

Interviewer:	OK that's everything thank you very much – that's very helpful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What 'A' levels did you do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Maths – maths at 'AS', physics and English Lit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and what type of school did you go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Bog standard

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It wasn't an all girls school?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No – comprehensive school

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, I did like a two weeks placement, you know – like your normal work experience that you do at sixth form I did in an engineering place.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What do your parents do? Are either of them engineers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, my dad's not technically an engineer, he's a design draughtsman, but it's kind of – he works for an engineering firm.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, sort of in the industry. OK when and why do you think that you decided to do engineering at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, well after my placement – I decided to do my placement – because the first placement I did was accounting and it was so boring – completely be boring and I was like I want to do something mathematical but more applied, so if you go down the physics line as well, its going to be the obvious choice isn't it. And because, once you've got an engineering degree, you don't have to be an engineer (OK) so I'm keeping it open.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh good, do you think anything else influenced your decision to study engineering, like your interests or the fact that your dad was in industry or any careers advice that you've had?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: My dad tried to put me off it, if anything, because he really hates his job. Erm, careers advice was – well, non-existent really. There was nothing to it. I suppose it was my own decision but I really don't know on what influenced it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Your dad didn't put you off though?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. Well after I'd done my placement I was like yeah, this is so much more interesting than the stuff you're doing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you decided you did want to do engineering, did you do much research into it, or did you speak to any other engineers or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I kind of got in touch with a guy, who got me my placement and basically what he said was, you know, get an engineering degree then you've got so many options that you're not tying yourself down – so go for it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, What do you think it is that appeals to you about engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, probably the hands-on ishness. It's not just sat in a lab, you do get to do other things as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, why do you think you decided to do mechanical engineering and not civil engineering or something in one of the other disciplines? Did you ever consider doing any of the others?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I considered electrical, cos I kind of want to do mechatronic, but I couldn't find a uni that did a good mechatronic course, whereas mechanical you get mechatronic elements in it anyway. So it's like if you select those modules, you can get mechatronics basically.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what is it – that specifically? You know, about – mechatronics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, toys.- play (?) – I suppose it's like – it's new technology, isn't it really – things like something to play with, I'm such a little kid.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you applied to the course, did you know you wanted to do a placement year?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. [This university] was my last choice.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: (?) and it was well, it was, [university 2] was my first choice and they wouldn't take me. And [this university] had already confirmed that they'd take me basically, whatever I got, so I rang them up and they were like yeah, so I thought I'll just go to [this university].

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Were you upset that you didn't get to go to [university 2] though?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, not really. Erm, I wasn't actually that bothered between all six anyway anyway. But [university 2] had a better reputation than [this university] because it had the lowest grades but I figured wherever I went it'd be good fun.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you realise that engineering was so male dominated when you decided to do it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does it ever bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Nah, at school like my maths class I was the only girl. In physics there was two of us, you get used to it. I did electronics at GCSE, I was the only girl on that – it really didn't make a difference.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not purely because they're female. If they're gonna be good engineers they'll go for it but …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women don't do engineering, not because they don't even know what it is, to be interested in it in the first place?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I guess quite a lot of places – a lot of people wouldn't think of it or suggesting it to the girls. Whereas, my school – they kind of give you the chances and they knew what I was like anyway. But yeah, it could be like more education or…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, What characteristics then, do you think make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, probably slightly strange (laugher). You've got to like playing with things and playing about with things and practical. Anyone who sits down and takes something apart – basically will make a good engineer, cos they'll know how things will work. I suppose that's (?) – you have to know what makes things work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that men are generally more like that than women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well some are but then some women are like it as well. I guess it's the way you've been brought up rather than the natural male/female thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there is a perception though?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I guess so. If you break something you take it to daddy, not mummy don't you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, Do you think that there are any advantages or disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Loads of advantages.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: If you're sat in a lab, and you can't do it, and you go, I'm really stuck, and I don't really understand – they'll help you. All the lads are just like, he didn't tell me that. You're like well, tough. Yeah, you can get away with a lot more, and I think there is a perception that you've done more as well, so they'll give you more help, they will. And girls don't mind asking, in like the group of us there's like me and [name] and then there's like 6 lads and they'll be like oh I'll work it out now, and if you just ask they'll tell you and – but none of the lads'll ask, so you do get away with more but then you add something as well so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what about any disadvantages?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Sorry?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any disadvantages?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well I guess it's the same that you're perceived to be dumber, so depending on what company you're applying to, and what lecturers you've got and stuff. I know there's one lecturer who does sort of go, ooh, you're a girl, and again I suppose if you're applying for jobs you might be disadvantaged but then again, a lot of people are looking for female engineers now, aren't they? So it's usually an advantage.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, in terms of the course then, has it been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Pretty much – yeah. I mean I went through a lot of it on open day and stuff anyway but…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How many women are on your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, 15 maybe – I don't really know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Out of how many?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think 20. It seems really high.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That's fine. What would you say have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Best things are design modules because you get to play. The worst things is Maths, because it's just pure calculations and no application whatsoever.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is it hard then to see how it fits in with everything?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Well some of it, you can see how it fits in. Some of it you're like we did this at 'A' level and it didn't apply to anything then and we're doing it again and it still doesn't apply to anything now.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: On the whole though, are you pleased then that you did choose this course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. It's going to be a degree worth having, rather than I don't know, walking out with something that you haven't put any effort into and you're just…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How many?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: One, I think. The – might be one in the first year. I think there is only one so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the female lecturers have a different style of teaching or have you noticed that they teach a different type of subject or do you not sort of like …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don't mean to generalise with you know, her –but she was very hormonal, she was pregnant. So, yeah, she taught for (thermo?) and we have like 6 (thermo?) lecturers and she was one of them. But she didn't teach the easy bits, by any means.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, not a lot – I'm not really bothered. The percentage of girls on the course, you expect it to be the same for lecturers really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the lecturers treat the students equally? You've said a bit already about some of them.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Most of them will, up to a point. I mean if you blatantly push the fact that you're a girl – they will treat you differently.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do many people on your course do that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There is some really girly girls. My house mate was a really girly girl, but she dropped out. But she was like all pink, blonde, get away with anything kind of girl. But yeah, no not really. I mean some of them do but you don't know if it's just cos you're you, or cos you're female. 'Cos they treat everyone differently anyway, I don't really think it's a male/female thing, it's more of a what you push sort of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you got a personal tutor then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: He's male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you get on with them, are they approachable?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, he's lovely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, you wouldn't rather have a female tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'm not bothered at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, probably my tutor because he understands what it – you know, I failed a module in my first year and I rang him in the middle of the summer holidays, and he was like, you knew you'd fail one of them anyway, and he was really cool and…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So he encouraged you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, he was really practical as well, he was like you know, you failed it but you know you've got a back up, you know you can do it, now you've got one exam to revise for all summer, get on and do it, type of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK have you had to do much group work as part of your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yes, I've had a few projects.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you like doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Depends who you do it with. The groups you pick are fine because you get (reasonable?) people – if it's one you've been put into, it's like really frustrating if you're put with people that really don't care.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How often do you get put into groups and how often do you get to choose?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think you get about 3 projects a year and this year we've been – well one of them we completely chose, one of them you sort of – you can choose out of so many people, one of them they picked completely for you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, so it's mixed.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it's pretty even.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you get to choose who you want to work with then, how do you decide who to work with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I basically work with people you sit with in lectures – so I've got – well I did have 3 housemates – and people who lived next door – 3 house mates and then there's 4 other people as well and we usually just pick randomly between ourselves, for (?) or whatever.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and do you have a preference whether you work with men or women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Nah, I usually work with [male student] 'cos he's clever.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, again I think it just depends on the personality of the people. I mean they obviously do, but I think it's me as me rather than me as a female that makes the difference.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you had any particularly bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not yet. We've had better groups than others but we've been lucky in that every group's just had like 1 person that doesn't care, so everyone else just covers for them, whatever and it doesn't make a lot of difference. I'm sure if you're put in a group and there's like 3 people that didn't care and me, I'd be right!

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think are like the benefits of doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think if you get stuck you've got someone else to do it for you, basically. But it's not all your responsibility. If you work together you can get anything done, can't you?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it will benefit you when you go to work in the industry, as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It should do. I don't know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is there anything about the teaching or advice that you've had that will help you when you go on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well a lot of – just like – I suppose it's projects that help it because you're going to be on projects, on placement, so I guess it's them that's gonna effect you know, how you go about problems and stuff like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you will use a lot of the technical stuff as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well from what I've heard from other people, it's – none of the technical stuff applies. They completely – they teach you what they want you to know, they don't really bother with the theory at all, it's your other skills that they go on.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the course should be geared more for preparing you for going into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it'd be impossible, really purely because of the number of different placements there is – if you geared it towards say automotive placements and everyone else would be completely screwed anyway, so if you do it generally you know. I mean you obviously are gonna use some of the stuff we've learnt, it's just not all of it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, Do you feel like you're ready and prepared to go on placement really?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I'm fine. To get out and do something, for a change.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that, the way that you're taught, and the whole educational experience will reflect what it's like, at all, in industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think will be different?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: 9 till 5, Monday to Friday. Even the whole, having to be there and – 'cos with lectures you can kind of get there and sleep through a few and not really pay attention. You know what you're getting – this is a business lecture and it's going to be boring, whereas in industry it's going to be non-stop. I mean you're like gonna get slack periods and stuff, but you're gonna have to work, from the time you're there, is the impression I get. But then, I'm basing this on most people – I know quite a lot of older people, like people who graduated last year and stuff that did placements – I'm basing this on quite a lot of theirs.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you found it helpful talking to people that have the experience of working?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah – yeah, definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they people that are your friends sort of anyway?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, well my boyfriend's an engineer, but he's a chemical engineer and there's quite a lot of people in Canoe club who were on placements last year, or the year before or whatever, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, Why do you think you wanted to go on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: So much fun - Just to get out and do something practical and learn something real rather than sit down and do – I mean the theory is like – it's got to be useful otherwise we wouldn't be learning it, I guess but it does seem a bit irrelevant and our projects, like well, yes, I 'm setting you this project, but we know what the answer is because we did it last year and the year before that and the year before that, whereas in industry, you know, it's something new that you're doing and it's actually got some value to someone.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it'll help you put into context all the stuff you've learnt, as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'm sure it should do. We'll see.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, has anyone particularly encouraged or discouraged you from going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, my tutor told me it'd be good. My dad told me – I think my dad told me it'd be good. Erm, but yeah it was basically people who'd been on it before – they were like you know, it's such a good experience you know. You don't come back with any money but you know so much more, you know, and you're ready to get a job.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you know anyone that's chosen not to go on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that they decided not to do a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well he chose not to because he paddles for England and basically he spends so much time, out in – I think he took a couple of years out before he started uni and stuff like that to compete – so it's time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you don't know where you're going on your placement yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I do know, I'm going to [company] (lost words)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and what attracted you to them?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, well originally and honestly I applied to anyone that looked like it could be fun. I didn't bother on the whole, I thought yeah that'd be a good place and then I went that'll be – you know – it would look good on my CV that, I want to have had an interesting year. And they have so much variety and you know they send you round the different departments – all engineering, so you weren't like spending hours in management or anything, so you got to see different parts of what they did, so – so I wasn't really sure what I want to do when I graduate, so I thought if I go there, get a good experience and then it might – at least it narrows it down like I don't want to do that or I do want to do that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, so you think it will help you decide what you want to do when you finish? Er, so there'll be quite a lot of variety in what you're doing as well. OK, where did you find out about the companies that you applied to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It was all through erm [placement co-ordinator].

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK are you happy with all the help that the university's given you finding a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think they give you loads of help. Apart from the fact that I wasn't on the list to start off with so I got all the emails.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that they should be doing anything else to help?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I think – if you go to the office and ask they're really helpful and basically they shouldn't be handing it to you on a plate. If you want to know stuff, you should have to get off your bum and go ask – they send you the original emails, so if you're interested and you want to know more, you should have to actively go and find out about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It does sound like your department actually gives quite a lot of help, compared to some of the other departments?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well Chem eng. They match you up with them, and say like you go to one interview and you've got it made. At least we have to apply.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: People in design technology are only just compiling their CV's and stuff.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Really? Yeah, well we do a lot of – I suppose it's 'cos they've got such good links anyway, in industry, that they get so many people actively coming to the uni, and saying, have you got any engineers that we can have, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That's really good. What sorts of things are you hoping to get out of your placement then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the whole working experience, basically. I really don't know what to expect, because I was like do you know what I'll be doing like – they were like we don't know what projects will be in when you start, so you have to wait and see, but the actual experience of work and real life.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you'll have the opportunity to use what you've learnt, when you come back for your final year?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I hope so. I don't know whether I actually will because it depends on how many projects I do as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Might what you do on placement help you make your mind up what you're going to do for your end of year project

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I expect it will decide me one way or the other. If I really hate it I'll know I won't do that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think will be the worst and best things or what are you most looking forward to and most worried about on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I'm looking forward to just getting in there and actually doing something, and having responsibility and stuff. I'm not really worried about anything, at the moment. I'm sure when I get closer I will be, but at the moment, it's a couple of months away and it's sort of like (??)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and do the company take other students or will you be the only one?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah there's – well there's 2 departments and there's 2 guys over the road, I think, and 2 guys with me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that will be useful having other students there?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, well it gives you like people to rent a house with and stuff – there's that. They're obviously used to taking on students so they know how to treat them and stuff, which is – you know, basically, you're not the first one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Have you found somewhere to live yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. But the give you like the first 4 weeks to sort it out, so basically you go into bed and breakfast - they pay for it and everything, you're just like we'll get together then and look.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that you'll get treated differently, being at work to being at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: What you mean – yeah – you're gonna – hopefully, they're gonna treat you like a proper employee and give you responsibility and you know expect you to do it, whereas here you get the impression that's it's just like well, oh they're students, you know, they're lazy and they're not gonna bother sort of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you're working do you think that they will treat you like another student or ..?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well judging by people who are there – there was two people on placement there, that we talked to when we went for interview and they were like yeah, you know, give you stuff, sit down and get on with it, and if you can't – you know, they help you through it but they expect you to pave your own way, sort of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK, in terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Up North. Not working down south. Erm, yeah, hopefully I'll be chartered and earning money.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, what about say in 10 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Doing the same things, hopefully earning slightly more money but yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, would you like to go into management?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Stay on the more technical side?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, one because I'm a technical expert – I don't ever want to do management.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what then would be your ideal career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Playing with robots. I really want to play with robots, just like all day every day.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that a realistic option in what you want to do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Yeah, well if you went across to the mechatronics rather than the mechanical (yeah) it's very feasible that you could do something like robotic arms or something anyway – maybe not normal robots but yeah, robotic arms going to need (??)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that now you'll encounter any difficulties at all, trying to achieve that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'm sure I will. But I dunno what they'll be but it's not going to be pie on a plate.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, would you like to work abroad at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, if they speak English, I'll be fine. I'm not really that bothered. I go travelling when I go paddling abroad and stuff, erm and if they want to send me abroad that's fine but …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in engineering at the minute?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I hope so. Erm, yeah I guess so. You're always going to need engineers aren't you?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about once you're in the industry for like moving up the career ladder? Do you think the opportunities are good there?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I guess it's the same as everyone else's at the time I want to move.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's fine - are you happy with all the career choices that you've made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'd do slightly more work at 'A' levels. Not to go to a different uni, but just so I knew the stuff now, because now it's just like, well, I know I did that but I can't actually remember, and having to go back and re-learn that before you do the other stuff. Yeah, I'd do more work – apart from that….

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, technical, erm hard working – that's 2 – slightly crazy.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You'll always get – 'cos you get very involved people. You know you get the slightly eccentric lecturers, like we had one today that had got a rice pudding tin, drilled a hole in it, got the rice pudding out, filled it with like some sort of fuel and he set a match to it, in the middle of the lecture and we were like – great one – and it's like oh, I should have safety goggles on for this but never mind. You always get the slightly eccentric people and I think you seem to get more eccentric engineers than most other things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you describe it as masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I suppose I should – I suppose I should, yeah, but I don't see it like that but I don't know if that's 'cos I'm trying to sort of integrate into it, but I'm trying to block myself seeing it like that sort of thing – you know deny the fact that its masculine – but I suppose it is, just the sheer numbers.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it is just the sheer numbers of males in the industry that make it masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Or is it the type of work that's being done and the whole sort of ingrained culture?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well it is kind of the ingrained culture but it is over 50 years. If you had half and half male/female you wouldn't still say oh it's masculine, because the females have taken over. It is yeah – it really is the culture but it's because it's male that the culture's like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, you said earlier that one of your house mates dropped out and that she was a girly girl, do you think that there's like this perception that if you are a woman and that you're an engineer, women can look after the height of femininity a bit to get on.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: And we see – she was well lazy anyway, so she was never gonna make it, but then [Sophie] (pseudonym), you've met, she's like a girly girl as well – she does the whole (?) and stuff, she's a really good engineer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's fine. Do you think the fact that it's masculine, will cause any problems at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don't think it will now. I think it might have done 10 years ago, but now people are leaning towards female engineers. So, there's more men about you know, actively trying to employ them, to get the numbers of accepting them in more, and everywhere you go there's probably already been a female engineer that – before you – who's like paved the way. But yes, you don't have so much work to do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that maybe women sometimes do have to work harder, to prove that they can do it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In certain situations yeah. Especially if you are the first or one of the first. I know when I went on my work experience placement and I first went down to shop floor. There was quite a lot of engineering (?) but when you went down to the fitters there weren't any. Well, at the first day that was when I was proving, yeah, I could do exactly what they could do and you know, I could wander round in my boiler suit and my hard hat and have a go just like them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think the situation will improve for women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, just cos of the sheer number, yeah. Every year there's more women going into it, and in theory, in the end you should get half and half, shouldn't you?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you think that your educational experiences differ from other students, say in humanities or social sciences?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I do more work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that's the main difference or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: What do you mean?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the fact that you have to do more lectures and things like that, do you think that will help prepare you more for going into the industry, the fact that you have a more structured timetable?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, in certain ways, yeah but in other ways they've got to do more reading on their own because I suppose it's gonna be easier to work on your own. I think the way the course is structured helps you what – going into the industry that it's made for, so I suppose that's the difference.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK that's everything thank you very much – that's very helpful.
